title: IQP Inspections for Access-Controlled Doors: The Compliance Check Most NZ Building Owners Overlook
description: Every access-controlled door in a New Zealand building with a compliance schedule carries a legal obligation under the Building Act — an annual inspection by an Independently Qualified Person, or IQP. The door must be inspected, tested, and reported to the local council each year, confirming it is performing to its specified standard. In practice, most building owners either do not know this applies to them, or they leave it until a compliance failure surfaces during a council audit. Red Wolf holds IQP qualifications and carries out these inspections as part of a broader access control service. We check that each door is latching, locking, and releasing correctly under all conditions — including alarm activation and power failure. If it is not performing to standard, we fix it and issue the required documentation. With the end of the calendar year approaching, now is a practical time to check whether your compliance schedule is current. If you are not sure whether your doors need an inspection, we can tell you in a short conversation what is required and what it will cost.

title: A New Study Found That Less Than Half of Organisations Are Confident in Their Active Assailant Response — Here Is What NZ Businesses Should Do About It
description: ASIS International and Everbridge released research this week showing that less than half of respondents are highly or mostly confident their staff know what to do in an active assailant incident. Four factors were linked to higher confidence: a comprehensive written plan, regular drills, communications technology, and a functioning behavioural threat assessment and management team. The gap between having a security system and having a prepared organisation is exactly what this finding describes. A camera at the front door and a monitored alarm panel do not tell your staff what to do when something happens. Physical security has two components — the technology layer and the human layer. Most businesses invest in the first and largely ignore the second. The organisations with the highest confidence in their readiness have both: documented procedures, tested regularly, supported by the right technology, and owned by someone with the authority to act. If your business has never run a scenario exercise or reviewed its emergency response documentation, that gap is worth closing before you need it.

title: Survey Finds 91% of Customer-Facing Workers Faced Aggression Last Year
description:
On 28 October the NZSA signed the ShopCare Retail Pledge, formally recognising occupational violence and aggression as a critical risk in New Zealand retail. The pledge follows the ShopCare National Customer Aggression Survey, which found that 91% of customer-facing workers experienced customer aggression in the past year. On the same day, ASIS International released its revised Workplace Violence Prevention and Intervention Standard.

For Auckland and Wellington retailers, this moves aggression out of HR and into site security, and it needs a designed response. The physical measures matter. Duress buttons should reach a monitored response. Counter and back-of-house layouts should give staff a safe exit. CCTV should capture faces at entry and point of sale. Access control should keep stockrooms and cash areas restricted to staff. Technology alone doesn't solve the problem. The ASIS standard treats prevention as a programme with clear roles and continuous improvement, and the electronic layer should support that plan rather than replace it. Staff need to know what each system does and what happens after they press the button.

If your team is dealing with escalating incidents, send us a message to book a site review focused on staff safety.

title: Three Checks Procurement Teams Should Run on Security Integrators Before Award
description:
Procurement teams in Wellington and Auckland often send us the same brief: we need a security integrator we can trust on site, and we need to justify that choice to our board. Price comparisons rarely answer that question.

Our approach is to make the evidence easy to check. Red Wolf is a member of the New Zealand Security Association. The NZSA represents over 85% of the NZ security industry by revenue, and its stated objective is an industry made up of fit and proper persons and firms. For a buyer, membership is a starting point, not the whole answer. We recommend three checks for any provider. First, confirm current NZSA membership directly with the association. Second, ask how technicians are vetted and certified before they work on your site. Third, request references from comparable deployments. We include all three in our tender responses, so evaluators aren't chasing documents after the deadline. The outcome for the buyer is a shortlist built on verifiable standards, and a decision that holds up when audit or the board asks why.

If you're preparing a security tender, send us a message and we'll send through our membership and vetting details.

title: Before the Christmas Shutdown: What's Your Biggest Unresolved Security Gap?
description:
Last week we published our poll results on the biggest physical security gap in NZ businesses. Our takeaway was simple: you can't fix the gaps you haven't found. With two months left in the year, that is the question worth answering before sites go quiet.

Over the New Zealand summer shutdown, many Wellington and Auckland premises sit empty or lightly staffed for weeks. Faults you could live with during business hours become real exposures. Think of a door that doesn't latch, a camera nobody has checked since winter, or an alarm zone that was bypassed and never restored. Access cards may still be active for people who left during the year. Our position is that a year-end review should be a short, practical walkthrough, not a report that sits in a drawer. Check what is installed, confirm it works, remove what shouldn't be there and fix the faults before the team leaves.
